text:
Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth.

Glass at room temperature is an amorphous solid, not a slow liquid. Estimates of its room-temperature viscosity (Zanotto, 1998; refined by Zanotto and Gupta) put the time for noticeable flow at far longer than the age of the universe. Your windows will break, fog, or get replaced long before any measurable sag.

The thick-bottomed church panes come from how the glass was made. Medieval crown and cylinder glass came out uneven, and glaziers often set the heavier edge at the bottom for stability. Some old panes are installed thick side up or sideways, which flow couldn't produce. Older glass objects also show no deformation: Roman glassware and centuries-old telescope lenses are as precisely shaped as when they were made.
